source.credit: The same Foucault pendulum, from a stretch the filmmaker sped up 5× (1:05.5–1:28 of the original); we cropped out the on-screen 5× label before the run. Zátonyi Sándor (ifj.), FizFilm

stated_facts.said: This Foucault pendulum is 8.97 metres long.

subjects.description: large shiny spherical metal pendulum bob with dark top suspension swinging along a floor line

observation.what_happens: A large silver metal ball hung as a long pendulum swings back and forth along a tiled floor line between a near red marker and a far blue marker. The oscillation continues uninterrupted throughout the clip, moving away from the camera to the far end and returning to the near foreground repeatedly.

calibration.note: no ruler needed: the swing is measured as an angle

pivot.why: the distances from the pivot split into two bands (bimodality 0.58), so the path is not one circle

given: pendulum length = 8.97 m (“This Foucault pendulum is 8.97 metres long.”)
pendulum length L = 8.97 m (stated): hold L fixed and measure g
reasoning: The theta trace shows a regular back-and-forth oscillation about ~1.56 rad with slowly shrinking amplitude and a slow upward drift of the minima and centre. These are the classic signs of a long pendulum in air with weak damping plus a drifting plane. Candidates therefore go from textbook undamped gravity swing to viscous, quadratic-air-drag, and drifting-centre versions to predict the held-back decay and drift.

critique.finding: The ball swings like a damped pendulum pulling with {g} and losing energy to friction {gamma} around centre {theta0}. It only partly captures the motion and leaves a regular wobble in its misses.
critique.headline: Long pendulum swings on, air friction barely matters.
critique.why_it_won: It keeps a steady swing with a touch of friction while the undamped swing wanders far off and extra drag terms add nothing.

headline: Long pendulum swings on, air friction barely matters.
finding: The ball swings like a damped pendulum pulling with 242.86 ± 0.14 m/s² and losing energy to friction 0.0047 ± 0.0031 1/s around centre 1.56672 ± 0.00060 rad. It only partly captures the motion and leaves a regular wobble in its misses. That is 25× stronger than Earth’s gravity, so the clip most likely plays about 5× faster than real life.

eyeball.confidence: low-medium, period timing is clear for g but amplitude scale and damping rely on assumed tile size and short observation window
eyeball.law_in_words: Small-angle simple pendulum period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) with L=8.97 m, amplitude A = L*sin(theta0) decaying as exp(-gamma*t), T timed frame-by-frame from near-to-near passages at 13.3 fps.

clock.note: Gravity came out 25× too strong: the clip probably plays about 5× faster than real life (time-lapse or dropped frames).

truth.note: Real footage of the same pendulum, from a stretch the filmmaker sped up 5× and labelled on screen; we cropped the label out before the run. The length (8.97 m) and period (6.0 s) are the figures the filmmaker published with the video on Wikimedia Commons; Ansatz was told the length and nothing else.
